title: A Commons by Decision
paragraphs: Technologies are rarely judged by the circumstances of their release, yet those circumstances often determine what the technology becomes. The World Wide Web offers a clear case. The history of its release therefore deserves more attention than it usually receives.

Its origins were modest. In March nineteen eighty nine, Tim Berners-Lee proposed at CERN a distributed information system to ease the sharing of documents among physicists; he resubmitted a lightly edited version in May nineteen ninety, and by the end of that year a server and a browser were running. The first website, hosted on Berners-Lee's own computer, described the project itself. In hindsight, the modest scale of the project concealed its eventual importance.

Nothing in those early achievements settled who would control the result. Many contemporary networked services were owned and governed by single organisations, and the Web could readily have joined them. The decisive act came on thirty April nineteen ninety three, when CERN's directors signed a statement placing the Web software in the public domain; a later release in nineteen ninety four adopted an open source licence. A different decision that day would have changed the lives of millions of later users.

The consequences of that choice are difficult to measure but easy to imagine. Because no one needed permission, a student, a hobbyist, or a start-up could publish, experiment and compete with established institutions. That openness did not guarantee quality, honesty or fairness; it guaranteed only access. Freedom to publish is not the same as freedom from harm, and the difference has become a permanent theme.

Access, however, proved to be an extraordinarily powerful foundation. It is one reason why the Web is often described as a commons: a shared resource whose value grows with use. Whether it remains one depends on choices as deliberate as the one made in nineteen ninety three.
